questions.q: For three positive integers& $p, q, r$,~$x^{pq^{2}} = y^{qr} = z^{p^{2}r}$~and~$r = pq + 1$~such that $3, 3\log_{\mathrm{y}}x, 3\log_{\mathrm{z}}y, 7\log_{\mathrm{x}}z$are in~ A.P. with common difference~$\dfrac{1}{2}$. The~$r - p - q$is equal to&
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Let

$x^{pq^{2}} = y^{qr} = z^{p^{2}r} = \lambda$

Then,

$pq^{2} = \log_{\mathrm{x}}\lambda$

$qr = \log_{\mathrm{y}}\lambda$

$p^{2}r = \log_{\mathrm{z}}\lambda$

So,

$\dfrac{\log_{\mathrm{y}}\lambda}{\log_{\mathrm{x}}\lambda} = \dfrac{qr}{pq^{2}}$

$⇒ \log_{\mathrm{y}}x = \dfrac{r}{pq} . . . \left(1\right)$

Similarly,

$\log_{\mathrm{x}}z = $\dfrac{pq^{2}}{p^{2}r} = \dfrac{q2}{pr} . . . . \left(2\right)$

$\log_{\mathrm{z}}y = $\dfrac{p^{2}r}{qr} = \dfrac{p2}{q} . . . \left(3\right)$

So,~$3, 3\log_{\mathrm{y}}x, 3\log_{\mathrm{z}}y, 7\log_{\mathrm{x}}z$~are in A.P., hence~$3, \dfrac{3r}{pq}, \dfrac{3p^{2}}{q}, \dfrac{7q^{2}}{pr}$~are~in A.P. Therefore,

$\dfrac{3r}{pq} -3 = \dfrac{1}{2}$

$r = \dfrac{7}{6}pq$

Also,

$r = pq + 1$

So,

$pq + 1 = \dfrac{7}{6}pq$

$⇒ pq = 6$

$⇒ r = 7$

So,

$\dfrac{3p^{2}}{q} =3 + 2\left(\dfrac{1}{2}) =$4$

$⇒ $\dfrac{3p^{3}}{pq} =$4$

$⇒ p^{3} = 8$

$⇒ p = 2$

$⇒ q = 3$

Hence,~$r - p - q = 7 - 2 - 3 = 2$

$

questions.q: Let $a$ and $b$ be two distinct positive real numbers. Let ${11}^{th}$ term of a GP, whose first term is $a$ and third term is $b$, is equal to $p^{th}$ term of another GP, whose first term is $a$ and fifth term is $b$. Then $p$ is equal to
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given,

${1}^{st}GP ⇒ \text{First term} = a, {a}_{3} = b$

$⇒ ar^{2} = b$

$⇒ r^{2} = \dfrac{b}{a}$

$⇒ {a}_{10} = ar^{10} = a \left(\dfrac{b}{a}\right)5 . . . \left($i\right)$

${2}^{nd}GP ⇒ $\text{First term} =$a, {a}_{5} = b$

$⇒ aR^{4} = b . . . \left(ii\right)$

$⇒ {a}_{p} = aR^{p - 1}$

$⇒ {a}_{p} = a \left[ $\left(\dfrac{b}{a}\right)\dfrac{1}{4}]p - 1 . . . \left($ii\right)$

Now, using the given condition of $p^{th}$ term we get,

$⇒ $a $\left(\dfrac{b}{a})5 = $a \left(\dfrac{b}{a}\right)\dfrac{p - 1}{4}

$⇒ \left(\dfrac{b}{a}\right)$5 = \left(\dfrac{b}{a}\right)\dfrac{p - 1}{4}

$⇒ 5 = $\dfrac{p - 1}{4}

$⇒ p = 21$

$

questions.q: The sum of all two digit positive numbers which when divided by $7$ yield $2$ or $5$ as remainder is
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Two-digit numbers of the form $7\lambda + 2$ are $16, 23, 30, . . . , 93$

These number are forming an arithmetic progression with first term~$a = 16,$~common difference~$d = 23 - 16 = 7$~and last term~$l = 93$

And, we know that the last term of an arithmetic progression is given by~$l = a + \left(n - 1\right)d$

$⇒ 93 = 16 + \left(n - 1\right)7$

$⇒ 77 = \left(n - 1\right)7$

$⇒ n = 12$

Two-digit numbers of the form $7\lambda + 5$ are $12, 19, 26, . . . , 96$

Again, using the last term of $A . P . ,$~we get~$96 = 12 + \left({n}_{1} - 1\right)7$

$⇒ 84 = \left({n}_{1} - 1\right)7$

$⇒ {n}_{1} = 13$

Now, the sum of~$n$~terms of~an~$A . P .$~is~${S}_{n} = \dfrac{n}{2}\left(a + l\right),$~we get~the sum of all the above numbers as

$= \dfrac{12}{2} \left(16 + 93\right) + $\dfrac{13}{2}\left(12 + 96\right)$

$= 654 + 702 = 1356 .$

$

questions.q: If in a G.P. of $64$ terms, the sum of all the terms is $7$ times the sum of the odd terms of the G.P, then the common ratio of the G.P. is equal to
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
For the given GP, $n = 64, {S}_{n} = 7{S}_{o}; \left\{\text{where}{S}_{o} \to \text{Sum of odd terms}\right\}$

$⇒ a + ar + {ar}^{2} + {ar}^{3} + . . . + {ar}^{63} = 7 \left(a + {ar}^{2} + {ar}^{4} \ldots . . + {ar}^{62}\right)$

$⇒ $\dfrac{a\left(1 - r^{64}\right)}{1 - r} = \dfrac{7a\left(1 - r^{64}\right)}{1 - r^{2}}

$⇒ \left(1 - r^{64}\right) = $\dfrac{7\left(1 - r^{64}\right)}{1 + r}

$⇒ 1 = $\dfrac{7}{1 + r}

$⇒ 1 + r = 7$

$⇒ r = 6

$

questions.solution:
$\mathrm{T}_2+\mathrm{T}_6=\frac{70}{3}\mathrm{ar}+\mathrm{ar}^5=\frac{70}{3}\mathrm{~T}_3 \cdot \mathrm{T}_5=49\mathrm{ar}^2 \cdot \mathrm{ar}^4=49\mathrm{a}^2 \mathrm{r}^6=49\mathrm{ar}^3=+7, \mathrm{a}=\frac{7}{\mathrm{r}^3}\mathrm{ar}\left(1+\mathrm{r}^4\right)=\frac{70}{3}\frac{7}{\mathrm{r}^2}\left(1+\mathrm{r}^4\right)=\frac{70}{3}, \mathrm{r}^2=\mathrm{t}\frac{1}{\mathrm{t}}\left(1+\mathrm{t}^2\right)=\frac{10}{3}3 \mathrm{t}^2-10 \mathrm{t}+3=0\mathrm{t}=3, \frac{1}{3}$
Increasing G.P. $\mathrm{r}^2=3, \mathrm{r}=\sqrt{3}\mathrm{T}_4+\mathrm{T}_6+\mathrm{T}_8=\mathrm{ar}^3+\mathrm{ar}^5+\mathrm{ar}^7=\operatorname{ar}^3\left(1+\mathrm{r}^2+\mathrm{r}^4\right)=7(1+3+9)=91$

questions.q: Let the sum of the first $n$ terms of a non-constant $A . P . , {a}_{1}, {a}_{2}, {a}_{3}, . . . . , {a}_{n}$ be $50n + \dfrac{n ( n - 7 )}{2}A,$ where $A$ is a constant. If $d$ is the common difference of this $A . P .$, then the ordered pair  \left(d, {a}_{50}\right)$ is equal to$
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given sum of& $n$ terms is~${S}_{n} = 50n + \dfrac{n\left(n - 7\right)}{2}A \ldots ( 1 )$

$⇒ {S}_{n - 1} = 50 ( n - 1 ) + \dfrac{( n - 1 ) \left(n - 8\right)}{2}A \ldots \left($2\right)$

Subtracting~$( 1 ) and $( 2 ) ,$~we get

${S}_{n} - {S}_{n - 1} = 50n - $50\left($n - 1\right) + $\dfrac{n\left(n - 7\right)}{2}$A - $\dfrac{\left(n - 1\right)\left(n - 8\right)}{2}$A$

$⇒ {S}_{n} - {S}_{n - 1} = 50 \left($n - n + 1\right) + $\dfrac{A}{2}\lleft(n \left(n - 7\right) - \left(n - 1\right)\left($n - 8\right)\right)$

$⇒ {S}_{n} - {S}_{n - 1} = 50 + $\dfrac{A}{2} \left($n^{2} - 7n - n^{2} + 9n - 8\right)$

$⇒ {T}_{n} = {S}_{n} - {S}_{n - 1} = 50 + A ( n - 4 )$

Hence,~${T}_{1} = 50 - 3A$~and~${T}_{2} = 50 - 2A$

$⇒ d = {T}_{2} - {T}_{1} = A$~and~${T}_{50} = 50 + 46A .$

$

questions.q: Let ${S}_{1}$ be the sum of first $2n$ terms of an arithmetic progression. Let ${S}_{2}$ be the sum of first~$4n$ terms of the same arithmetic progression. If  \left({S}_{2} - {S}_{1}\right)$ is $1000$, then the sum of the first $6n$ terms of the arithmetic progression is equal to:$
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
${S}_{2n} = \dfrac{2n}{2} \left[2a + \left($2n - 1\right)d\right], {S}_{4n} = $\dfrac{4n}{2}\left[$2a + \left($4n - 1\right)d\right]$

$⇒ {S}_{2} - {S}_{1} = $\dfrac{4n}{2} [$2a + ( 4n - 1 ) d ] - $\dfrac{2n}{2} \left[$2a + \left(2n - 1\right)d\right]$

$= 4an + ( 4n - 1 ) 2nd - 2na - ( 2n - 1 ) dn$

$= 2na + nd [ 8n - 2 - 2n + 1 ]$

$⇒ 2na + nd [ 6n - 1 ] = 1000$

$2a + \left(6n - 1\right)d = \dfrac{1000}{n}$

Now, ${S}_{6n} = \dfrac{6n}{2} \left[2a + \left($6n - 1\right)d\right]$

$= 3n $\cdot \dfrac{1000}{n} =$3000$

$

questions.solution:
Given,

First term of A.P are& $1, 2, 3 . . . . 10$, so general term of the first term~will be~$i$

And common difference are~$1, 3, 5, . . . .$, so general term of common difference~is given by~$2i - 1$

Now sum of the A.P ~is given by,

${S}_{i} = \dfrac{12}{2} \left[2 \timesi + \left($12 - 1\right)\left($2i - 1\right)\right]$

$⇒ {S}_{i} = 6 \left[$2 \timesi + 11 \left(2i - 1\right)\right]$

So,~$\mathop{∑}_{i = 1}^{10}{S}_{i} = \mathop{∑}_{i = 1}^{10}144i - 66\mathop{∑}_{i = 1}^{10}1$

$⇒ \mathop{∑}_{i = 1}^{10}{S}_{i} = 144\left(\dfrac{10 \times 11}{2}) -$66 \times10$

$⇒ \mathop{∑}_{i = 1}^{10}{S}_{i} = 792\left(10\right) - 66 \times10$

$⇒ \mathop{∑}_{i = 1}^{10}{S}_{i} = 7260$

Hence this is the correct option.

questions.q: If the sum and product of the first three terms in an $A . P .$~are $33$ and $1155$, respectively, then a value of its ${11}^{th}$ term is:
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Let, the first $3$ terms of the~$A . P .$~are $a - d, a, a + d$

$⇒ sum = 3a = 33 ⇒ a = 11$

And product \left(a - d\right)a\left(a + d\right) = a\left(a^{2} - d^{2}\right) = 1155$

$⇒ 11\left({11}^{2} - d^{2}\right) = 1155$

$⇒ 121 - d^{2} = \dfrac{1155}{11} = 105$

$⇒ d^{2} = 121 - 105 = 16$

$⇒ d = \pm 4$

For $a = 11, d = 4,$ the $A . P .$~is~$7, 11, 15, \ldots$

The~$n^{th}$~term of an~$A . P . ,$~with first term~$A$~and common difference~$d$~is~${T}_{n} = A + \left(n - 1\right)d$

So,~${T}_{11} = 7 + 10 \times 4 = 47$

For $a = 11, d = - 4,$ the $A . P .$~is~$15, 11, 7, \ldots$

So, ${T}_{11} = 15 + 10\left(- 4\right) = - 25 .$

$

questions.q: In an A.P., the sixth term ${a}_{6} = 2$. If the ${a}_{1}{a}_{4}{a}_{5}$ is the greatest, then the common difference of the A.P., is equal to
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given: ${a}_{6} = 2$. Also, ${a}_{1}{a}_{4}{a}_{5}$ is greatest.

$⇒ a + 5d = 2 . . . \left(i\right)$

Let, $y = {a}_{1}{a}_{4}{a}_{5}$

$⇒ y = a ( a + 3d ) ( a + 4d )$

$⇒ y = ( 2 - 5d ) ( 2 - 2d ) ( 2 - d )$

$⇒ y = \left(4 - 4d - 10d + 10d^{2}\right) \left(2 - d\right)$

$⇒ y = \left($4 - 14d + 10d^{2}\right)\left($2 - d\right)$

$⇒ y = 8 - 4d - 28d + 14d^{2} + 20d^{2} - 10d^{3}$

$⇒ y = 8 - 32d + 34d^{2} - 10d^{3}$

$⇒ y^{'} = - 32 + 68d - 30d^{2}$

$⇒ y^{'} = - 2 \left($15d^{2} - 34d + 16\right)$

$⇒ y^{'} = - 2 ( 5d - 8 ) ( 3d - 2 )$

So, the function attains maxima at $d = $\dfrac{8}{5}

$

questions.q:
The sum of the common terms of the following three arithmetic progressions.

$3, 7, 11, 15, \ldots \ldots \ldots \ldots , 399$

$2, 5, 8, 11, . . . . . . . . . 359$ and

$2, 7, 12, 17, \ldots \ldots , 197$, is equal to _____ .
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
We have,

${S}_{1}: 2, 5, 8, 11, . . . , 359$

Common difference is~${d}_{1} = 3$

${S}_{2}: 3, 7, 11, 15 . . . , 399$

Common difference is~${d}_{2} = 4$

${S}_{3}: 2, 7, 12, 17 . . . , 197$

Common difference is~${d}_{3} = 5$

Now taking~$LCM$~of common difference we get,

$LCM\left({d}_{1}, {d}_{2}, {d}_{3}\right) = 60$

So, common terms are $47, 107, 167$,

Hence, the sum will be~$47 + 107 + 167 = 321$.

questions.q: The sum of first four terms of a geometric progression  \left(G . P .\right)$~is $\dfrac{65}{12}$ and the sum of their respective reciprocals is $\dfrac{65}{18} .$ If the product of first three terms of the $G . P .$~is $1,$ and the third term is $\alpha,$~then $2\alpha$ is _________.$
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Let number are $a, ar, ar^{2}, ar^{3}$

$a \left(r^{4} - 1\right)r - 1 = $\dfrac{65}{12} \ldots \left($1\right)$

\dfrac{1}{a} $\left(\dfrac{1}{r4} -1)\dfrac{1}{r} -1 = \dfrac{65}{18}$

$\dfrac{1}{ar^{3}}\left(\dfrac{1 - r^{4}}{1 - r}) = \dfrac{65}{18} \ldots \left(2\right)$

\left($1\right)\left(2\right) ⇒ a^{2}r^{3} = $\dfrac{3}{2}

and~$a^{3} \cdotr^{3} = 1$

$ar = 1$

\left(ar\right)2 \cdotr = $\dfrac{3}{2}

$r = $\dfrac{3}{2},$a = $\dfrac{2}{3}

So, third term$= ar^{2} = $\dfrac{2}{3} \times \dfrac{9}{4}

$\alpha = $\dfrac{3}{2}

$2\alpha =3$

$
